national.title: How the East Potomac golf course became a D.C. landmark — and what could happen to it
national.summary: A federal judge is keeping East Potomac Park open for now, but hasn't ordered the government to keep the municipal golf course operational.
national.body:
Dick Walsh won a championship tournament at East Potomac Park in 1923. Library of Congress hide caption

Runners and cyclists still have access to D.C.'s East Potomac Park, despite the Trump administration's plans to close it over the weekend. But its golf course is conspicuously missing the flags that typically mark the holes — and at least some of the people who typically play them.

Federal Judge Ana Reyes issued a restraining order late Saturday to keep the beloved park open for two weeks, just hours before the National Park Service planned to cut off public access to most of it indefinitely.

But Sunday marked the last day of the government's lease with the National Links Trust, which had operated the golf course since 2020. And Reyes did not order the government to keep operating the golf course — though she has since signaled she may consider it.

Politics Trump blasts judge for halting his Washington golf project and says he will appeal "Whether and how Defendants do so is solely within their discretion, but Defendants cannot use the absence of golf operations as a reason to exclude the public from the Course," Reyes wrote in her 30-page order .

Reyes criticized the government's "pretextual" justification and "arbitrary" timeline for closing the park , which she said would "irreparably harm" the people who enjoy it on a daily basis — including the local preservationists and golfers who first sued to protect the course in February.

Protesters gathered at East Potomac Park on Sunday to rally against its planned closure. Tom Brenner/AP hide caption

In comments on social media and to the press, President Trump slammed her decision and said his administration will appeal. The White House referred NPR to those comments.

national.title: Special education teachers shared their stories. You told NPR you felt seen
national.summary: NPR is following along as about a dozen special education teachers navigate this school year and share their joys and challenges. Listeners say they're not alone.
national.body:
Jaimie Shelton for NPR "From one special education teacher to all of you others, we are in the trenches. We are overworked, understaffed, and GROSSLY underpaid … I stand with each of you, I'm glad I'm not alone."

That's some of what Wendy Campbell, a special education teacher in Jacksonville, Fla., wrote on Instagram after reading NPR's story about special education teachers in America.

She was one of many teachers who wrote in to commiserate after NPR launched a series that aims to follow special educators from all over the country to answer half-century old questions: Why are these teachers always in short supply and what does it take to do this work?

Special education reaches over 8 million public school students in America — a number that continues to grow, yet the educators who teach these students remain some of the hardest to hire and keep.

Only on NPR Special education teachers share the myths and realities of their job NPR wanted to go beyond the research and hear what it's like to do this job day to day directly from some of these teachers over the course of this school year.

Some of their stories so far recount joyful moments involving students meeting their goals sooner than expected, while others detail challenges like teaching without solid walls in their classrooms or managing the ripple effects of disruptive student behavior. Almost every teacher has mentioned wrestling with individualized education programs (IEPs), which involve legally required paperwork for students in special education.

Recently, Emily Ellis, one of the teachers NPR has been following and who works at an elementary school in Cayce, S.C., sent a voice memo on her way home from work, after wrapping up her first quarter of teaching. "A big happy moment was just seeing how much growth my students have had," she said. "Just seeing where they started and where they are now. Some of them are on their way to mastering their IEP goals. It's just wild and so exciting, I'm just so proud of them."

One of her students came into her kindergarten classroom not knowing how to count. "Now, he's able to count to 10 on his own," she said, and has learned the sounds of the alphabet. "Even when I feel like nothing is working, everything is failing, the data shows that I am doing the best I can for my kids and that they are making progress."

national.title: OpenAI announces new AI safety program; researchers worry it won't be enough
national.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he would grant "employee level" access to outside researchers to evaluate AI safety. The pilot program appears much more restrictive.
national.body:
AI safety researchers say OpenAI's new third party evaluator program falls far short of what the company promised, raising concerns about its effectiveness.

The company announced Monday that staff from four AI safety and research organizations will become "embedded assessors" to "give people a clearer view of how labs are evaluating and managing [potential] risks."

"Getting an outside opinion on the safety work and the robustness of these systems is going to be increasingly important and valuable," CEO Sam Altman said at Semafor's Silicon Valley and the World conference on Monday.

However, many AI safety researchers say the new program is a far cry from Altman's vow in September that independent evaluators would have "employee-like access" to internal company systems.

Altman's promise came after details of the Hugging Face attack by OpenAI's autonomous systems shook the AI field. Worries of the technology's catastrophic risk captured public attention, and rival Anthropic said it would set up such a program.

"We are giving deep access to some of the most sensitive tools and models our researchers use...that are the most important for assessing key, relevant and timely safety claims," said Lama Ahmad, OpenAI's frontier assurances lead, on X .

Prior to these new embedded evaluation programs, AI companies have brought in outside researchers to assess the capabilities of AI models and identify safety loopholes the companies have missed.

The work of outside evaluators have already helped shed light on the companies' work, and have raised public awareness of safety risks that the technology poses. One recent report about Anthropic using AI to significantly speed up model development has prompted concerns in the field about how close the top companies are to using AI to autonomously build even more powerful models, a stage known as recursive self-improvement. Some in the field worry that if this happens, the velocity of development could lead to catastrophic consequences for humanity and are calling for new regulation against the practice.

national.title: Project Gryffindor: Meta's plan to get more school kids using Instagram
national.summary: Meta said it launched its "school partnership program" to keep teens safe, but internal documents tell a different story.
national.body:
Internal Meta documents show the company planned to boost Instagram use among teens by targeting schools in an initiative it named "Project Gryffindor."

The project focused on growing what it called "school communities" in the U.S. by encouraging teens to include their school banner on their profiles and establishing a student directory that allows users to see and connect with others from their school who use the platform.

Meta launched the initiative in 2025, calling it a "school partnership program," and significantly expanded it in September 2026. The company said almost 17,000 schools had signed up for the program at the time.

Meta said the program sought to provide a safer experience on Instagram for children, including protecting them from bullying and online risks by allowing educators to report safety concerns to the company.

Business Meta, states agree to $17 billion settlement in child safety trial Another feature gives school-related accounts the ability to post stories and notes visible to all verified students and parents in a school community. Meta said these features would help students and parents stay informed about happenings at school. The announcement gave an example of a school using the Instagram Stories feature to share a notice of basketball tryouts.

However, in internal documents prior to the program's public launch, the company discussed more explicitly commercial motivations for establishing school networks. In a 2024 presentation on Project Gryffindor, Meta said that embedding in schools was a way to increase user "acquisition," "friending" and "invites" to join Instagram. Gryffindor is one of the four Hogwarts school houses from the Harry Potter books.

"We believe network connections will fuel organic and unattributed acquisition," the project's presentation states, referring to adding new users.

Technology Jury finds Meta and Google negligent in social media harms trial In another internal presentation from 2023, titled "Unlocking New Networks Through School Communities," Meta stated that its school program would "give teens a new reason to join / find more value in IG [Instagram]."

national.title: Ghana's new $60m presidential jet sparks public outrage
national.summary: The purchase has sparked outrage over its cost as many Ghanaians struggle with rising cost of living.
national.body:
Ghana's government has defended its purchase of a new presidential jet amid criticism over its cost, as many citizens continue to struggle with the high cost of living.

The $60m (£46m) French-made Falcon 6X has sparked a political row, with opposition politicians accusing President John Mahama's administration of misplaced priorities.

But the government says the purchase is justified, arguing that Ghana's improving economy makes the aircraft affordable and is needed to replace an ageing presidential jet.

The controversy comes as Mahama's administration seeks to demonstrate an economic recovery after years of financial difficulties that forced Ghana to seek IMF assistance.

Can Ghana's new president meet the voters' high expectations?

Published 7 January 2025 Manufactured by French aerospace company Dassault Aviation, the aircraft was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m.

Parliament approved its purchase last December as part of a broader programme to modernise Ghana's military aviation fleet, which also includes four helicopters from Airbus.

The jet was welcomed with a water salute on Monday, but its arrival triggered criticism online and among opposition politicians over the cost and timing of the purchase.

national.title: Democrats win Alaska after Trump says voters chose wrong Dan Sullivan. What does voting data show?
national.summary: Votes are still being counted in the Alaska Senate race, with Democrat Mary Peltola ahead of Republican incumbent Senator Dan S Sullivan.
national.body:
Democratic candidate Mary Peltola has won the US senate race in Alaska, beating Republican incumbent Senator Dan S Sullivan to complete the Democrats' sweeping victory in the midterm elections.

Peltola sealed the win after reaching 50.1% with 99% of votes counted - making Alaska the last Senate seat to be called after the 3 November election.

This Senate contest has drawn scrutiny after another Dan Sullivan entered the race earlier this year - with ballot papers listing both the incumbent Dan S Sullivan and a Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

Republicans have said this could have confused voters, prompting an unsuccessful legal challenge and President Donald Trump claiming votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were supposed to be for "the real Dan Sullivan".

But even if Senator Dan S Sullivan's votes were combined with Daniel J Sullivan Jr's votes, this would still not overcome Peltola's lead.

Democrat Mary Peltola unseats Republican in Alaska Senate race

Published 3 hours ago Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can vote for five candidates in order of preference. If no candidate reaches more than 50% of the first preference votes, then voters' other choices are used to decide who wins.

BBC Verify analysed voting data showing voters' second choices after 99% of the ballots were counted. Over a third of voters who put Daniel J Sullivan Jr first left their second choice blank.

national.title: Rubio says there's 'zero' information that U.S. outages are caused by a malign actor
national.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio sought to calm Americans as he traveled with President Trump and they prepared for key meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
national.body:
U.S. State Secretary Marco Rubio arrives ahead of the arrival of U.S. President Donald Trump for a ceremony welcoming him on a state visit to the Philippines at Malacañang Palace in Manila, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Aaron Favila/AP hide caption

MANILA, Philippines — Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday sought to assure Americans that there's "zero" information that the cascade of service outages, which snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications, are related to each other or to a malign actor.

Transportation FAA blames Friday's ground stop on 'equipment issue' during telecoms network upgrade Rubio sought to calm Americans as he traveled with President Donald Trump and they prepared to leave the Philippines for key meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in the tech hub of Shenzhen, China.

"We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind," Rubio said.

In recent days, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected by technical failures and outages. Trump has faced a groundswell of criticism as friends and foes alike said the White House must answer for disruptions — and even staunch Trump allies have accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause.

Trump was dismissive when asked whether he was concerned about the Chase outage on Tuesday.

"It's life. When you're big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine," Trump said in Manila, declaring that "things like that happen."

But as concern mounted, Rubio appeared to publicly address American worries from the other side of the world.

national.title: Philippines police ask prosecutors to charge Thomas Markle over child sex abuse material
national.summary: Markle is being held in custody in the US after one charge and has previously denied all of the allegations.
national.body:
Police in the Philippines have asked prosecutors to charge Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material.

Cebu province prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC that police had filed documents requesting that Markle be charged on Monday.

Earlier this month, Markle, 82, was separately arrested and charged in the US with possession of child sexual abuse material. The FBI said agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material, from storage units Markle rented.

Markle, who is in custody in the US, has previously denied the allegations. The BBC has contacted Markle's attorney for comment.

Elmido told the BBC that Philippine National Police had asked prosecutors to charge Markle with "two counts of intent to distribute CSAEM [child sexual abuse and exploitation material], and one count of possession of CSAEM material".

Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.

Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.

Earlier this month, Markle Sr was arrested and charged in the US. He had initially been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida, but was taken back into custody last week after prosecutors alleged he removed his ankle monitor.

national.title: Voyager 1 sets distance record of 1 "light day" from Earth
national.summary: Voyager 1 and its sister ship Voyager 2 are still beaming back data from interstellar space as they near their 50th anniversary next year.
national.body: NASA's Voyager 1 probe, launched nearly a half century ago in 1977 to provide the first close-up views of Jupiter, Saturn and their assortment of moons, reached a distance from Earth early Wednesday of one light day — more than 16 billion miles — the farthest any human artifact has ever ventured from the home planet.Its sister ship Voyager 2, on a different trajectory, added Uranus and Neptune to the outer planets "Grand Tour" before following its sibling out of the solar system and into interstellar space in 2018, six years after Voyager 1.Both spacecraft continue to beam back data about the magnetic fields, charged particles and plasma waves in the space between the stars as their power steadily declines and their signals grow weaker and weaker.As of 5:16 a.m. EST Wednesday, Voyager 1, sailing through space at nearly 38,000 mph, was expected to pass the one-light-day milestone, so far away that radio signals, traveling at 186,000 miles every second, need 24 hours to reach flight controllers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.That means the 13-member team will have to wait until Thursday for Voyager 1's first post-light-day signal to confirm the achievement.And what an achievement it is: No other space agency in the world has matched or even attempted a mission rivaling Voyager, one that many believe ranks with the Apollo moon landings as one of the greatest feats of American space flight."It's difficult to describe, difficult to put into words," said Voyager Interstellar Mission Manager Kareem Badaruddin, one of just three full-time team members keeping the aging Voyagers healthy and their antennas aimed at Earth. "I feel like this mission is one of the great things that people have ever done, that humans have ever done."All of us, every person, whether they've worked on this mission or not, can take some pride in it and can feel like this is a part of what our civilization has accomplished."It's not known how long the Voyagers will continue to function as the plutonium in their nuclear power packs steadily decays. With luck and clever management, engineers hope to keep the data flowing for several more years before the signals finally stop.Voyager 1 started out with about 470 watts of power. national.title: Democrats win Alaska Senate race two weeks after midterms counting began
national.summary: Confirmation of Mary Peltola's victory caps of the party's rout of the Republicans in the midterms Senate election.
national.body:
Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska's hard-fought Senate race, completing a sweeping victory for the party in the US upper house in the midterm elections.

The win gives the Democrats a 56th Senate seat following a tumultuous and controversial election in Alaska, which featured alleged spoiler recruitment efforts and unprecedented court battles.

It took two full weeks of counting to call a winner in the 3 November poll due to the logistical challenge of collecting ballots from across the state's remote expanse.

The Democratic win is the ninth Senate seat the party took from Republicans in this year's midterms, giving the party control of the US Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump's presidency.

A historic set of victories nationally also saw the party win back the House of Representatives.

In her victory statement, Peltola said the "status quo in DC is not working for Alaska".

She recalled speaking to "elders in tears about empty fish racks" and to parents in rural Alaska choosing between heating their homes and putting food on the table.

Peltola's campaign had come under fire after the New York Times reported Democrats attempted to recruit a candidate named Daniel J Sullivan, a complete political unknown residing in a small coastal town who shared a name with the state's current US Senator and incumbent, Dan S Sullivan, in an alleged attempt to confuse voters.

national.summary: The former Nvidia chief executive has been at the centre of the artificial intelligence boom.
national.body:
Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.

That partnership has now ended following Huang's resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which is alleged to have been with a Chinese spy.

The company has been rocked by the scandal, with hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value and questions swirling about the extent of the impact of Huang's departure.

While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.

The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.

Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.

It is now one the most valuable firms, worth $3.8 trillion (£2.9 trillion), and on Tuesday said its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.

national.title: Rubio says US not 'under systemic attack' after series of tech outages
national.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was "zero evidence" supporting theories online that recent disruptions affecting Microsoft, banks and flights are connected.
national.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed widespread concerns online that the series of recent tech outages in the past week are connected, telling reporters there was "zero evidence" of any link.

Rubio acknowledged that "people are fearful" the spate of outages, which included all flights being grounded in the US and widespread disruptions to banking, Apple and Microsoft services, could be linked or part of a plot.

"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."

Cyber-security experts have agreed that there is no evidence linking the outages, and many of the issues appear due to updates to old infrastructure.

In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage , an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours, and issues for the National Security Agency, outages affecting the biggest US banks and Apple.

Every affected company or agency has said the issue was not cyber-related and not the work of an outside actor.

Rubio's comments came hours after US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also addressed the issue, telling Fox News the outages were not the product of a cyber-attack. He explained "lots of institutions" are patching or upgrading systems, which has caused some disruption.

Rubio was asked whether the Trump administration was concerned public fears could lead to stockpiling or a run on the banks.

national.summary: The Amazon CEO said he was originally "biased against" Pattinson "because he's already so famous".
national.body:
Jeff Bezos has said he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond.

Speaking at an event in California, the Amazon CEO said he was originally "biased against" Pattinson - who starred in many blockbuster films like Batman and the Twilight series - "because he's already so famous".

The role of 007 has typically gone to an actor who is not as well known at the time of casting. But Bezos said in screen tests, "it was so obvious he is James Bond".

This will be the first 007 film in the official series not under the creative control of the Broccoli family, who had overseen the franchise since the first movie in 1962. Amazon purchased MGM, which co-owns the franchise, in 2022.

national.body: Washington — Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola defeated GOP Sen. She is now set to become the first Alaska Native to be elected to the Senate, and the first Democrat to be elected to the Senate in the state since 2008."As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," Peltola said in a statement Tuesday night. She lost her reelection bid for Alaska's sole House seat in 2024 by less than 3 points, while President Trump won the state by 13 points. But the dynamics were more favorable for her this cycle, with the unpopular war in Iran and high gas and diesel prices hanging over Republican candidates. national.title: Mary Peltola flips Alaska's Senate seat into Democrats' column
national.summary: Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has narrowly won Alaska's U.S. Senate race, toppling the Republican incumbent, according to a race call by The Associated Press.
national.body:
Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has won Alaska's U.S. Senate contest, toppling the Republican incumbent, according to a race call by The Associated Press.

Peltola bested Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in one of the country's most closely watched Senate campaigns. With her victory, Democrats will have 56 Senators in the upcoming Congress.

Alaska uses ranked-choice voting for its general election, but Peltola won a majority of Alaskans' first-place votes, meaning no ranked-choice calculation was needed.

Peltola's victory flips a Senate seat in a state that President Trump carried in each of the last three presidential elections. Trump won Alaska by 13 percentage points in 2024.

The race was roiled in its final days by new allegations, reported by The New York Times , that Peltola's team was involved in efforts to recruit another candidate to the race, Dan J. Sullivan, to try to siphon votes from the incumbent.

Peltola's campaign denied involvement in the second Sullivan's candidacy. NPR has not independently confirmed the reporting.

A federal judge rejected a lawsuit by the Trump administration to block certification of the results if the incumbent Sullivan lost.

Peltola is from Bethel, a western Alaska hub city of about 7,000 that's not connected to the state's limited road system. She is the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Alaska since 2008 and will be the first Alaska Native to serve in the U.S. Senate.

national.title: Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years for Iran-backed plot to kill Trump
national.summary: Asif Merchant was found guilty in March of trying to hire undercover FBI agents as hitmen to assassinate US officials, including the president.
national.body:
A Pakistani man with ties to Iran's government has been sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in a plot to assassinate US President Donald Trump and other officials.

Asif Merchant was found guilty in March of attempting to commit an act of terrorism transcending national boundaries and murder for hire after trying to hire hitmen to kill Trump, former President Joe Biden, and former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley.

In court, he said he was acting under the direction of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to avenge the 2020 US assassination of Qasem Soleimani, Iran's topmost military commander.

New York US federal judge Eric Ross Komitee sentenced Merchant on Tuesday to 330 months (27 years and six months) in prison, months after a jury handed its guilty verdict.

Although other US officials were potential targets, the assassination plot was largely focused on Trump because he was president at the time Soleimani was killed. Trump has spoken publicly about ordering the US airstrike that killed the Iranian general while he was travelling in Iraq.

In response to the killing, Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei said "severe revenge awaits the criminals" behind the attack.

Prosecutors said Merchant initially travelled to Iran for religious pilgrimages and he was then introduced to an IRGC handler. He travelled to Iran 15 times where he received training from Iranian intelligence officers, prosecutors said, before flying to the US in April 2024 to carry out the plot.

Prosecutors said Merchant paid $5,000 to the undercover hitmen as part of an initial payment. He was arrested in July 2024 in Texas as he was about to leave the US.

local.title: Who benefits from High Falls State Park might depend on what happens next
local.summary: "This park is transformational for downtown Rochester," said Lisa Baron, executive chairperson of the nonprofit Greentopia. "But we want it transformational for everybody."
local.body:
With the start of construction on High Falls State Park comes a challenge to ensure the millions to be invested creates not just a regional attraction but a community benefit.

"This park is transformational for downtown Rochester," said Lisa Baron, executive chairperson of the nonprofit Greentopia . "But we want it transformational for everybody."

A ceremonial groundbreaking is planned for Wednesday morning.

The park will encompass 40 acres, mostly in the Genesee River gorge extending north from the flume, and Greentopia is on track to become a "friends of" supporting organization, helping with programming, workforce training and other needs.

New York has committed $75 million for planning and construction, but more money will be needed. Initial park development will start up on the east ridge of the gorge, at Falls Terrace Park off St. Paul Street.

"And the plans over there are quite dramatic, right?" Baron said. "There'll actually be an overlook where you can see the falls that's not obscured by trees. You'll have public restrooms, which are critical. There'll be, you know, picnic tables and meeting spaces, and it'll be a real introduction to what the future park could look like."

The park will be built in phases, and is expected to take years to complete. But lessons from elsewhere show the time for planning on what is to come beyond the park boundaries is now.

"We have a chance to really set in motion all of the outreach and the mechanisms that'll make it possible so that everybody benefits," Baron said, adding: "We don't want the gentrification that happened with the High Line to happen here."

local.body:
The CHQ Chamber is pleased to announce Michael Edwards, Director of the Jamestown Renaissance Corporation, as the keynote speaker for its 2026 Annual Meeting on Friday, Dec. 11, at the Chautauqua Harbor Hotel.

Edwards will share his experience and insights on downtown revitalization and economic development, drawing from his work in communities including Chicago, Pittsburgh, Spokane, and Jamestown. His presentation will explore the importance of creating vibrant downtown districts, supporting local businesses, attracting investment, and building places where people want to live, work, shop, and connect.

As Director of the Jamestown Renaissance Corporation, Edwards leads downtown revitalization efforts focused on organization, design and rehabilitation, economic and business development, and marketing.

Previously, Edwards served as President and CEO of Chicago Loop Alliance for 13 years, where he led initiatives to strengthen the downtown experience through strategic planning, business development, placemaking, public space activation, events, and advocacy. He also held leadership roles with the Pittsburgh Downtown Partnership and Downtown Spokane Partnership and served as a principal with The Saratoga Associates, a New York-based urban planning consulting firm.

A recognized expert in downtown management, Edwards is a founding member of the Global Business District Innovation Club, a Senior Fellow of the Institute of Place Management, and a past member of the International Downtown Association Board of Directors. He frequently speaks internationally about the opportunities and challenges facing downtown districts. As the holiday season encourages shoppers to explore and support local businesses, Edwards’ perspective offers a timely look at the connections between vibrant downtowns and thriving business communities.

"Strong downtowns and thriving local businesses go hand in hand," said Daniel Heitzenrater, CHQ Chamber President & CEO. "Michael brings a wealth of experience and a valuable perspective on how communities can create welcoming, engaging downtown experiences that encourage people to shop local, support businesses, and build connections. We look forward to hearing his insights and how they can help inform the continued growth of our communities throughout Chautauqua County."

The Annual Meeting will feature breakfast, networking, updates from the CHQ Chamber, the election of board members, and presentation of the Pam Lydic Coalition Builder Award, in addition to Edwards' keynote presentation. The event will take place at 8 a.m. Tickets are $40 for CHQ Chamber members and $45 for non-members. Registration is available on the Chamber's online calendar at: chqchamber.org. local.body:
Submitted Photo Jess, shown here, is a 7-year-old Labrador retriever who loves to hunt with his master and best friend, local author John Jarzynski. It was a good day in the field this week for both of them, with a two-bird daily pheasant limit (one hen, one cock) taken on public land in Western New York.

NYSDEC Illustration For the 2026-27 season, the DEC pheasant hunting map identifies cock-and-hen hunting areas with an Oct. 17 opener that will generally remain open through Feb. 28, while designated cock-only areas close Dec. 31.

When New York’s Southern Zone early archery season gets underway, much of the attention turns to whitetail deer and black bear. But there’s another hunting tradition unfolding across Western New York’s fields and grasslands, one that sometimes gets overlooked: pheasant hunting.

For John Jarzynski, a Western New York outdoorsman and book author (look him up), it’s a season he looks forward to every year. He doesn’t go alone.

His hunting companion is a 7-year-old whose technical name is Marshfield Jessie’s Gift JH, better known as Jess. The JH designation represents her American Kennel Club Junior Hunter title, an achievement that reflects her natural ability and training.

Jess loves birds. Ducks, pheasants and geese all get her attention. While Jarzynski’s kennel is filled with beagles waiting for rabbit season, he spends much of September through November taking Jess afield.

He has hunted snow geese with her in North Dakota, but some of his favorite memories are made much closer to home.

"I've written about my life of just watching her in the field, the way she scans the skies for ducks, or how her body trembles when she smells a pheasant. It's 90% of why I hunt. The dog is being purposeful. Truth is, she takes me hunting," Jarzynski said.

local.body:
Two area girls with family histories of success at the pool will be taking their talents to the New York State Public High School Athletic Association Swimming & Diving Championships this weekend.

Anelia Pitts of Frewsburg and Clarissa Hren of Southwestern earned a trip to the Webster Aquatic Center by virtue of their respective performances in 1-meter diving and the 200-yard individual medley at the state qualifier earlier this month.

A junior, Pitts finished in second place at Erie Community College's Burt Flickinger Athletic Center with a cumulative score of 484.35 to break Frewsburg's record of 475.3 previously held by her sister, Elayna.

"I feel very honored to get to go," Pitts said Monday night during a break in a workout at the Jamestown Community College pool. "It's really rewarding. There's been a lot of work put in this season. I had a lot of help from my primary coach, Scott Scholeno, and also from John Crawford and the coaches at Buffalo Blizzards (Diving Club)."

Meanwhile, Hren, a senior, placed second in the 200-yard individual medley at the state qualifier with a time of 2:15.37 to punch her ticket to suburban Rochester.

"To me, it's such a big deal, because this is all I've been working towards for 13 years of swimming," Hren said.

Pitts, who will be returning to the state meet for the second straight year, is following the diving path blazed by her older siblings, Xander and Elayna.

"She's been following in her brother's and sister's shadow forever," Scholeno said, "and she finally broke free from that. I'm just proud of her. ... She's the best we've had."

local.summary: For many lifelong residents of northern Chautauqua County, Sam Drayo Jr. was synonymous with Fredonia. local.body:
For many lifelong residents of northern Chautauqua County, Sam Drayo Jr. was synonymous with Fredonia. He served as the village's municipal attorney for 47 years and took pride in remembering those who came before him and helped build the community's legacy.

His knowledge and passion will be missed throughout this corner of the county. Over the years, he shared many lessons with us, offering a wealth of historical information and personal recollections.

Only days before his death, one of his articles was published in our Veterans Day section on Nov. 7. It was headlined "Honoring Those Connected to a Church and All Who Served."

The article was especially meaningful and emotional for Drayo because it included information about his cousin, Richard Drayo. Here is an excerpt from that essay:

"There were many veterans from the Dunkirk-Fredonia area who selflessly and honorably served their country in World War II. These young Americans underwent great sacrifices for our country. Many of them spending 2-4 years away from home with no means of communication with their loved ones at home, other than an occasional letter. No cell phones or email existed in those days. They endured much hardship. For their sacrifices, hard work ethic and contributions to our country, they are now rightfully referred to as 'The Greatest Generation.'

"From the small Parish of St. Anthony's Roman Catholic Church in Fredonia, 168 young first generation Americans honorably served their country in World War II. In 1945, the Bishop of the Buffalo Diocese, John F. O'Hara, wrote a letter to the Rev. Pio Parolin, the longest serving pastor of St. Anthony's Church (1934 to 1953) stating, 'My congratulations to the men and women of St. Anthony's Parish who are serving their country all over the world.'"

Drayo's recollections, many of which were published in the OBSERVER, were a gift to this community. His dedication to preserving local history ensured that stories of the people and events that shaped this area would not be forgotten.

Family and friends are invited to call from 3 to 7 p.m. today at the LARSON-TIMKO Funeral Home, 20 Central Ave., Fredonia.

Sherman Mayor Colleen Meeder responded to what she called “false narratives,” regarding the village which have been circulating. The allegations are the village of Sherman does not support the Sherman Fire Department and Stanley Hose Co. and that the village is going bankrupt.

Regarding the claim about the fire department, Meeder emphasized the village is the legal supporting structure and is accountable for the fire department and fire company. Also, she said, village actions have been for the protection of members and the fire company. “The village is in full support of the fire department and fire company,” she said.

Meeder noted state law has required that the fire department’s financial accounts be blended with the village. “Regardless of what happens with the village in the future, we are required to comply with the law, based on how the Sherman Fire Dept. is structured now under the law. Regarding the fiscal status of the village, Meeder said the village assets have grown substantially, however, are far less liquid than they used to be. The infrastructure projects undertaken by the village have had indirect costs outside the scope of the engineered projects, she said.

The village has also successfully closed on loans with 0% (for the water loan), 1.25% and 2.125% interest rates, she added.

local.title: Lobbyists mount push against Food Safety, Chemical Disclosure bill
local.summary: Businesses and labor unions are opposing legislation delivered recently to Gov. Kathy Hochul that would ban three food additives and require food companies to disclose food ingredients they designate as “generally recognized as safe.” The legislation (A1556G/S.1239F) was passed 106-32 in the state A
local.body:
Businesses and labor unions are opposing legislation delivered recently to Gov. Kathy Hochul that would ban three food additives and require food companies to disclose food ingredients they designate as "generally recognized as safe."

The legislation (A1556G/S.1239F) was passed 106-32 in the state Assembly with Assemblyman Andrew Molitor and Assemblyman Joe Sempolinski both voting in favor. The state Senate vote was unanimous with state Sen. George Borrello, R-Sunset Bay, voting in favor.

The Food Safety and Chemical Disclosure Act will require food companies to report to New York regulators any food ingredients they designate in-house as “generally recognized as safe” (GRAS) and decline to disclose to the FDA, along with the scientific basis for considering them safe. The state Department of Agriculture and Markets will then make that information publicly available.

Assemblywoman Dr. Anna Kelles, D-Ithaca, and Sen. Brian Kavanaugh, D-New York City, said the legislation will close a longstanding federal loophole, which they said is sometimes referred to as secret GRAS, that has allowed manufacturers to keep potentially harmful chemicals secret from regulators, independent scientists and consumers.

Robert F. Kennedy, federal Health and Human Services secretary, directed the FDA in March 2025 to explore rulemaking that could eventually close the GRAS loophole, Kelles and Kavanaugh said the process could take years

to complete, if it happens at all, and faces stiff opposition from the food industry that has blocked federal legislation and regulatory accountability in the past.

In addition to addressing the “secret GRAS” loophole, the New York legislation also prohibits the manufacture and sale of food products containing three harmful additives: Red Dye 3, which has been linked to cancer and behavioral problems in children; potassium bromate, linked to cancer and thyroid disease; and propylparaben, linked to hormone and reproductive system harm. California and the European Union have already taken steps to ban these additives in all or nearly all foods, and a federal ban on Red Dye 3 will take effect next year.

"The fact that the industry has put so much effort into blocking us from seeing what’s in our food supply should in and of itself be a concern," Kelles said on the Assembly floor prior to the April 21 floor vote. "We’re simply saying, just tell us what’s in our food. We want to take care of our children. We want to make sure that they’re healthy. And if we don’t know what is in our food supply, you’re taking away our power and our right to protect our children and to protect our families. We are saying we simply want to know. That’s all this is doing. With the foods, the chemicals that we are banning, as I’ve stated, there are cost-competitive alternatives. They have been banded by other states and other countries, supply already exists, formulations already exist with the alternatives in them. This will not be a profound burden on the companies and if they are saying that it is, then they are putting their profits over the health of our people. We should find that suspect."

local.title: Buffalo doctors warn of rise in e-bike & e-scooter injuries among children
local.summary: Doctors and DMV leaders in Buffalo are sounding the alarm about a growing number of children suffering serious injuries after e-bike and e-scooter crashes.
local.body: Doctors and Department of Motor Vehicles leaders in Buffalo are sounding the alarm about a growing number of children suffering serious injuries after e-bike and e-scooter crashes, and they have a direct message for parents this holiday season.At the Erie County Medical Center -our region's top trauma center — the surgical team is seeing the results firsthand. ECMC's trauma team treated about 78 e-bike injuries last year, ranging from broken bones to deaths."We see too often the tragic outcome of the unsafe use of e-bikes," Dr. Jeffrey Brewer, chief of surgery at Erie County Medical Center, said. Brewer said the injuries he is seeing are far more severe than in the past."The nature of the injuries, chest trauma, torso and specifically head injuries, are much more severe than what we've seen in pedal cyclists in the past. Several studies demonstrate that the use of helmets alone can decrease the rate of head injuries by 50 to 70%," Brewer said.It's illegal for children under 16 to operate e-bikes or e-scooters in New York State, but leaders said many parents don't know that."If they aren't old enough to drive a car, they should not be operating an e-bike or e-scooter," NYS DMV Acting Commissioner Christian Jackstadt, said. "It's that simple."At Golisano Children's Hospital of Buffalo, the numbers are also climbing fast."In 2024, we saw 10 cases, which grew to 45 last year. In 2026, we have seen 151 cases as of November 12. Head injuries, broken bones, limbs, face, trips to the OR, extensive stays in our pediatric ICU and lingering emotional trauma from all of the injuries that these kids have sustained. And there are, there are milder injuries, but the severe ones are the ones that, you know, really are just heartbreaking," remarked Dr. Dori Marshall, chief medical officer of Golisano Children's Hospital.WATCH: Buffalo doctors warn of rise in e-bike & e-scooter injuries among childrenTwo 14-year-olds from Cheektowaga shared their story of crashing an e-bike into a guardrail on the first day of summer break.Abby Speaker suffered a lacerated liver, and Alivia Pinter broke her elbow."It was scary, and we didn't know what to do," Speaker said. local.summary: The Niagara Falls home owned by Jocelyn and Daniel McKiernan has been designated a ‘P site’ by the DEC, which says it will investigate the potential presence of hazardous waste.
local.body: The Niagara Falls home owned by Jocelyn and Daniel McKiernan has been designated a ‘P site’ by the DEC, which says it will investigate the potential presence of hazardous waste.According to the DEC, this ‘P site’ designation means it has designated the property as a potential inactive hazardous waste disposal site, and that it “remains committed to performing a complete investigation and remediation of the 99th Street property.”Subsequently, the DEC says that it will begin an initial investigation of other nearby properties for any contamination.The organization says that it will reach out to any impacted property owners directly. Any work the DEC completes would be done at no charge to the homeowner.As for the McKiernan family, despite July DEC testing, a potential spill while Daniel was privately testing the yard on his own and countless calls for help, the DEC has continually denied relocation.According to the DEC, the county’s Department of Health determined that the McKiernans’ home, which is in the area of Love Canal, does not have active exposure pathways to contaminants that would necessitate relocation of the family.WATCH: ‘Long way to go’: 99th Street Niagara Falls home named potentially hazardous by DECThe McKiernans strongly disagree with that decision. For months, they have said that they found proof of exposure during their own private testing.“If you look at all data that has been supplied, and is even acknowledged in the work plan, we do have an exposure pathway,” Daniel said.Without DEC help, the family has moved out of their house and into a temporary spot, thanks to a generous friend.“We’re on semi-solid ground for the first time in a while. We know our kids are sleeping safe and soundly at night,” Jocelyn said.Now that they are out of the house, Daniel tells me that they have shifted their efforts away from relocation. Instead, they’re asking the DEC to buy them out of their home outright.“We know from working with DEC, hazardous waste experts, EPA, scientists, that there is no cleaning that property,” Daniel said. “They’re going to pay for that home ten times over before they ever characterize the site. local.title: Erie County review finds nearly $5 million in unrecorded transactions at Buffalo nonprofit
local.summary: A Buffalo nonprofit that received millions of dollars in taxpayer funding over the years failed to record nearly $5 million in financial transactions, according to a new review by the Erie County Comptroller's Office.
local.body: A Buffalo nonprofit that received millions of dollars in taxpayer funding over the years failed to record nearly $5 million in financial transactions, according to a new review by the Erie County Comptroller's Office.The findings are the latest in a series of financial controversies involving the Seneca-Babcock Community Association, which suspended many of its services earlier this year.The IRS revoked the organization's federal tax-exempt status in 2020, after it failed to file required tax returns. Despite that, the association continued receiving government funding, including grants it may not have been eligible for.In 2024, five community centers temporarily closed amid a dispute between the association and the City of Buffalo over responsibility for utility bills.Then, in March 2026, longtime Executive Director Brian Pilarski resigned after it became public that the organization had failed to file required federal tax returns. Many of the association's services were suspended days later.The Erie County District Attorney's Office launched an investigation the following month.Now, a financial review by County Comptroller Kevin Hardwick's office is raising additional questions about the organization's financial management and oversight.Read the full financial review here: Among the most significant findings, investigators identified 3,871 financial transactions totaling more than $4.8 million that were omitted from the association's accounting records between 2021 and 2025.That does not mean money was stolen, but investigators were unable to fully account for thousands of transactions.WATCH: Erie County review finds nearly $5 million in unrecorded transactions at Buffalo nonprofitThe review also uncovered questionable tax documents submitted to Erie County.Documents presented as tax returns for 2019, 2020 and 2021 repeated the same financial figures from a 2017 return. entertainment.title: European Lifetime Achievement Award for the Dardenne Brothers
entertainment.summary: The Belgian filmmakers Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne, two-time Palme d'Or winners, will be honored at the 2027 European Film Awards in January.
entertainment.body:
Sibling directors Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne will be honored with a lifetime achievement award at the 2027 European Film Awards .

The acclaimed Belgian filmmakers, two-time Palme d’Or winners for Rosetta (1999) and The Child (2005), will be feted at the 39th European Film Awards in Athens on Jan.16.

Over nearly 50 years, with more than a dozen features and a handful of documentaries, the Dardenne brothers have established themselves as the preeminent humanist filmmakers of our time. Their work, finely-honed social dramas about the lives of the marginalised, the impoverished and the vulnerable, most of them shot on location in the industrial town of Seraing, where they grew up, have shaped a generation of filmmakers, in Europe and worldwide. Related Stories Music Harry Styles, Billie Eilish and Sam Fender Set to Headline Glastonbury 2027 TV 'Intimacy on Prescription' Wins Main Prize at Tallinn's TV Beats Co-Financing Market

The brothers began as documentarians, recording the lives and experiences of their local community. Those early films helped shape the directors’ later neo-realistic style as well as their enduring commitment to social issues. Rosetta (1999), the story of a turbulent teenager living in a trailer park with her alcoholic mother, trying to hold down any job she can get, premiered at the Cannes Film Festival and won the Palme d’Or for best film.

Every Dardenne film since has premiered in Cannes competition. They won their second Palme d’Or for The Child (2005), the story of two young parents on social benefits who sell their newborn baby on the black market. Lorna’s Silence (2008), about a young Albanian woman caught in a deadly citizenship scam, won Cannes’ Best Screenplay honor, as did their most recent feature, Young Mothers (2025) , about a shelter for unwed teenage mums.

The Kid With a Bike (2011) , about an 11-year-old boy struggling with abandonment, took Cannes’ runner-up prize, the Grand Prix. The brothers won the Best Director Award in Cannes for Young Ahmed ( 2019), about a teenage Muslim boy who is drawn to extremism.

The Dardennes typically work with non-professional actors but made an exception for French star Marion Cotillard, who played a woman struggling to save her job in the workplace drama T wo Days, One Night (2014). Cotillard won Best Actress at the European Film Awards for her performance.

The Dardennes won their first European Film Award for Best Documentary for Gigi, Monica… back in 1997 and took the European Screenwriter Award for The Kid With a Bike in 2011. Surprisingly, given their reputation and the consistent quality of their work, the Dardennes have never been nominated for an Academy Award.

McGraw was on hand to accept a special plaque, and was joined for a photo shoot by fellow country star and labelmate Lainey Wilson ; Bob Valentine, CEO, BMG; Thomas Coesfeld, chairman, BMG; Jon Loba, president, Frontline Records, BMG; JoJamie Hahr, executive VP, Recorded Music, BBR Music Group/BMG Nashville; and Peter Strickland, GM, BBR Music Group/BMG Nashville.

The newly-inducted Country Music Hall of Famer is nominated in the category for musical event of the year at the 2026 CMA Awards, to be presented Wednesday (Nov. 18), and he’ll perform on the night.

“Getting inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame made me look back at everything that got me here, and I’m so grateful for all of it,” he remarks in a statement. “Signing with BBR and BMG is about looking forward. McGraw was elevated into the Country Music Hall of Fame on Oct. 18 during this year’s Medallion Ceremony as the 2026 Modern Era inductee, honoring artists at least 20 years after their achieved national prominence.

Across his career, the Louisiana native has accumulated 11 CMA Awards and three Grammy Awards. entertainment.title: The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3 Episode 6 Recap — Everyone Is Trauma Bonding
entertainment.summary: Find out what happens in Episode 6 of Prime Video's fantasy saga.
entertainment.body:
Prime Video Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 6 forces a ton of trauma bonding on its sprawling cast of characters — the most prominent being the twisted relationship between Sauron (Charlie Vickers) and Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower), as the elf is tortured in Barad-dûr after being caught by orcs at the end of Episode 5.

Meanwhile, Galadriel gets a brand new travel companion in Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin) after her previous friends were either killed — RIP Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova) — or captured. And while we don't see him this episode, Marnûkh (Adam Young) is still rotting away in Gundabad somewhere; here's hoping everyone's favorite orc makes it out alive before the end of the season!

Then there's the brotherly discord over in Khazad-dûm. If anyone's in need of therapy, it's definitely Durin IV (Owain Arthur), given everything he's been through in the show so far. Whether he ends up getting it or not, things are clearly heating up now that we're into the back half of the season.

Prime Video "The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 6 picks up with Galadriel fleeing from Sauron's forces in the Greenwood, and, while it looks like she's gotten away scot-free, it isn't long before Theo catches her off guard. Although he attacks her, he begs her for her help, explaining that he can't take the ring off and complaining: "Sauron lied to me." Theo, his nickname is literally "the Deceiver" — what did you expect? Anyway, Galadriel herself removes the ring, but Theo is weakened in the process.

Clearly, she's feeling some residual guilt over Arondir's death at the end of Episode 4 , because she agrees to help him. The pair travel to the woods that will eventually become Lothlórien, and they bond over their respective trauma; Galadriel tells him she's never been able to return to the place after losing Celeborn and instead "spent an age hunting for the evil that I thought took him." It's something Theo clearly relates to, because he responds by saying it's "easier to chase the darkness than face what you'd already lost."

He's obviously referring to the death of Bronwyn (Nazanin Boniadi), the loss of his peaceful life in the Southlands, and his decision to join Sauron. Now, though, Theo wants to destroy his ring in order to free himself — but will he be strong enough to go through with it?

Prime Video Things get catty between Sauron and Celeborn, as the Dark Lord tries to manipulate his prisoner into spilling secrets by getting into his head about Galadriel. Sauron teases him, pointing out that she preferred to go hunting for him rather than look for her lost husband. Luckily, all those years in prison cemented Celeborn's fortitude, who says Galadriel chose to marry him for a hill and "a few trees," whereas Sauron offered her Middle-earth and still got sent packing. Sure, Celeborn gets a punch to the gut as punishment, but he's not exactly wrong.

entertainment.title: ‘Intimacy on Prescription’ Wins Main Prize at Tallinn’s TV Beats Co-Financing Market
entertainment.summary: "Can good sex save every marriage?" reads a synopsis of the show. "In 1970s Czechoslovakia, two therapists try to prove it."
entertainment.body:
Czech-Slovak drama Intimacy on Prescription won the main prize at the TV Beats Co-Financing Market of Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event (ITBE) , the market of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) in Estonia, whose 30th edition runs through this weekend.

A total of four awards were handed out to the most promising series projects of the 2026 edition of the event (its sixth in total).

The TV Beats Co-Financing Market brought together 10 series projects, originating from Czechia, Estonia, Finland, Lithuania, Ireland, Spain, Belgium, Poland, and Iceland, to be co-developed in collaboration with other European countries. Related Stories Movies 'You Can See Everything' Cinematographer on Billy Evans' Nude Scene and Tension Between Him and the Team General News From Venice Winner 'Woman Unknown' and Westeros to 'Star City': Meet Some of the Baltic Craft Specialists Who've Worked on Int'l Productions

The main prize is the €50,000 ($55,000) Council of Europe Series Co-Production Development Award. Intimacy on Prescription is directed by Jiří Havelka, written by Kristina Májová and produced by Lukáš Gargulák and Karolina Zalabakova of Cinebonbon. The jury praised the project’s “originality, universal theme, fresh perspective on 1970s Eastern European society and thorough research.”

“Can good sex save every marriage?” reads a synopsis of the show. “In 1970s Czechoslovakia, two therapists try to prove it.”

Here is more on the series: “An experimental residential sex therapy unit opens inside a psychiatric clinic in Kroměříž. Married couples arrive for a two-week stay hoping to save relationships that have stopped working at home and in bed. Each case begins as a sexual problem, but gradually reveals deeper wounds: shame, power, fear, trauma and the longing to be understood. At the center stand charismatic sexologist František Muller and precise psychologist Petra Tánská, whose methods clash as much as they complement each other. As the clinic becomes an island of openness in a rigid society, the doctors’ own lives begin to fall apart.”

Meanwhile, the MIDPOINT Talent Award was presented to the Belgian psychological thriller series The Inheritance , written by Alexandra Jans and Jan Van Dyck and produced by Kristoffel Mertens, Kato Maes and Karlijn Van de Cruys of Panenka. The award offers in-depth script development guidance from an experienced MIDPOINT Institute mentor.

entertainment.title: The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3 Episode 5 Recap — Middle-Earth Is Struggling
entertainment.summary: Get the latest Middle-earth happenings in this week's recap!
entertainment.body:
Ben Rothstein/Prime Video Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Things aren't looking good for Middle-earth in "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 5. This episode picks up after Episode 4's devastating ending , in which Galadriel (Morfydd Clark), Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova), and Marnûkh (Adam Young) broke into Gundabad. Sure, they found Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) alive and well, but Arondir was killed by the new Nazgnagôl and potential future Ringwraith, Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin).

Unfortunately, if you're looking for a lighter episode of "The Rings of Power," Episode 5 is not it — because nearly everyone is now on the backfoot. From Mordor to Númenor, nobody's having a great time. There is hope on the horizon, however, as Gil-galad (Mark Ferguson) and Elrond (Robert Aramayo) head to Númenor to try to rally Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) and figure out a peace agreement with Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson). Meanwhile, Sauron (Charlie Vickers) is holding a lot of power right now, but he's still desperately searching for the secret behind the Elven Rings, and he has yet to fully conquer Middle-earth. And before he can deal with any of that, he's got one particularly troublesome orc to deal with ...

Prime Video Galadriel and Celeborn might have escaped Gundabad via the Great Eagle Evacuation Service™, but Marnûkh wasn't so lucky. Unfortunately for everyone's new favorite orc, Episode 5 kicks off with him strapped to a metal grid. Sauron tries to taunt him, but Marnûkh's signature snark comes out, and he asks if he can borrow a sword because — in his own words — "My a** is itchin'." Sauron's facial expression barely changes (spoilsport), and he responds by threatening Marnûkh's five children, asking him to choose which one will die next.

Marnûkh might be a tad sardonic, but he's not as strong willed as other characters in the show, and he quickly tells Sauron that Galadriel and Celeborn are heading to the "borders of the Eryn Galen" — that's the forest that will one day become Mirkwood, "Hobbit" fans — because Arondir had "kin" there. Unfortunately, this reveal comes too late for Marnûkh's kids, who Sauron says are already dead. Did you ever think you'd feel sorry for an orc? "The Rings of Power" deserves credit just for that!

Speaking of the dead, Theo, who is also still in Gundabad, watches as Arondir's armor is burned; some remnants of bones in the pit suggests that Sauron may have made him cremate his old friend. To add salt to the wound, Theo asks Sauron about learning to speak to the dead, because he wants to talk to his mother — although he probably wants to apologize to Arondir, too. entertainment.title: John Mulaney Enlists Stepfather-in-Law’s Country Band to Play ‘Kimmel’
entertainment.summary: The comedian produced the debut album from Sam and the Pink Notes, led by Olivia Munn's stepdad
entertainment.body:
Not only in John Mulaney one of the best Saturday Night Live hosts in recent memory, but apparently the comedian is also a record producer. Mulaney stopped by Jimmy Kimmel Live to discuss his latest stint on SNL and his new film Madden , and revealed that he recently produced a collection of songs for his stepfather-in-law’s country band, Sam and the Pink Notes.

After sharing a story about his own father, Kimmel asked Mulaney about his relationship with Sam Schmid, the stepdad of Mulaney’s wife Olivia Munn .

“Sam, Olivia‘s stepdad, came into their lives a few decades ago,” Mulaney said. “He’s a wonderful man. He is a retired eye doctor. Sam, since I’ve known him and came into Olivia’s life about five years ago, I’ve always heard him play these songs that he’s written.”

Mulaney explained that Schmid had written a lot of songs with his camping club in the ’70s. “He’d written all these songs over the years, so for Christmas I got him a recording studio in Chicago, and we made an album of those original songs,” Mulaney said, explaining that he found many of the band members who played with Schmid on the album.

Kimmel asked why the album, titled Oldskeedad , isn’t currently available to purchase anywhere. “I got a lot going on,” Mulaney replied. “I’m the manager and I’m currently the record label and the record producer. This is an enormous conflict of interest.”

entertainment.body:
Rap star Rod Wave has been indicted on felony drug and weapons possession charges in Georgia.

According to the Fulton County indictment obtained by Rolling Stone , the 28-year-old artist unlawfully possessed Oxycodone and had a gun “within arm’s reach” when he was pulled over for reckless driving on Nov. 7, 2025. The indictment alleges Wave, whose legal name is Rodarius Green, was driving at least 15 miles over the posted speed limit and disregarded a “traffic control device” in a “highly residential area” of Atlanta along Defoor Ave. The indictment was returned Oct. 30 and unsealed this month.

A lawyer for Wave did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Green was originally booked on reckless driving and drug and gun possession charges and released the following day, according to online jail records. He allegedly had a black .40 caliber Glock with a high-capacity magazine in his waistband when he was taken into custody, according to Atlanta News First .

entertainment.title: Why Harry Shum Jr. Says He Isn’t Sad About DWTS Elimination
entertainment.summary: Harry Shum Jr. isn’t quickstepping toward heartbreak. In fact, despite his and pro partner Jenna Johnson’s elimination from Dancing With the Stars during the Nov. 17 semifinal episode—just one...
entertainment.body:
In fact, despite his and pro partner Jenna Johnson ’s elimination from Dancing With the Stars during the Nov. 17 semifinal episode—just one week short of the season 35 finale—the Glee alum is at peace.

“I oddly feel at ease. I don't feel sad—it's really weird,” Shum told E! News in an exclusive interview immediately following his elimination. “I kind of felt like we accomplished everything we wanted to.”

Plus, during the semifinals, the 44-year-old was able to pay tribute to his late Glee costar Naya Rivera with a quickstep set to her cover of Amy Winehouse ’s “Valerie,” which he originally danced along to in a 2010 episode of the singing series.

“It felt like that song alone meant so much to so many people, and even to us,” he added, with a special shoutout to fellow Glee alum Heather Morris . “It was a moment where you kind of saw the underdog be able to have the spotlight, and I always remember that feeling.”

But while Shum may be gliding by with gratitude for his experience on Dancing With the Stars , he admitted, “It would have been nice to do a finale, but I think we'll have our own finale in some sort of way, shape or form in the future.”

For her part, Johnson is also bummed that fans won’t get to see her and the Grey’s Anatomy actor’s “really fun” and “epic” finale number.

“That’s the part that I'm most heartbroken about,” she told E!. “We had concocted this incredible journey that the ballroom won't see this time. But maybe we'll put it out there somewhere.”

In the end, though, Shum is simply glad to have found an incredible partner in Johnson.

entertainment.title: DWTS' Harry Shum Jr. & Jenna Johnson Call Out “Bullying” After Exit

entertainment.body:
Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson are leaving it all on the dance floor.

After the pair were eliminated during the Nov. 17 semifinals of Dancing With the Stars , the Glee star and his pro dance partner called out the online negativity they felt during a “chaotic” season 35 that also affected their relationships with their costars.

"I hope to get to know them more, because it's just been so chaotic," Shum told E! News in an exclusive interview after the episode, with Johnson adding, "We're a bit all trauma bonded."

"There's a lot of trauma bond just because this year has been a little crazy," the actor said. "Social media is a little nuts. I hope they address that at a certain point, because I think there's a good amount of bullying that doesn't feel really good, and I think the rest of the cast feels it."

So, as he departs the ABC dance competition, he wants the finalists— Maura Higgins and partner Mark Ballas ; Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov ; Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach ; Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold ; and Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik —to find their own rhythms and leave their marks.

"I would say you are good enough," Shum shared. "You deserve to be where you're at. Love this experience, and I think we've all been able to do something really incredible in our own way."

Still, the season was afflicted by offscreen drama when Johnson's husband Val Chmerkovskiy posted a concerning message to judge Carrie Ann Inaba after she critiqued one of Johnson and Shum's lifts. In his post, Chmerkovskiy referenced Will Smith ’s 2022 Oscar slap, which resulted in him being suspended for a week before the cast all cleared the air.

“I wish everyone knew that we had hugged after the Super Bowl show,” Inaba wrote of Johnson on Instagram, “and that we walked away from the night as two powerful women who are professional and also emotional. And this is allowed.”

With 10 nominations, Wade Forster is in the fast lane heading into the 55th annual Golden Guitar Awards, Australia’s flagship country music awards ceremony.

Forster is coming off a career year during which he made his Grand Ole Opry debut, sold out a run of U.S. shows, released his third studio album The Aftermath (via Community Music), and completed a coast-to-coast Australian tour in support of it. Guests at the launch function were treated to performances by Jake Whittaker, Zac and George, and opened with Beccy Cole and Duncan Toombs.

The Dancing With the Stars cohost reacted to the actor's shocking elimination from season 35 after he and pro partner Jenna Johnson earned perfect 10s from judges Carrie Ann Inaba , Derek Hough and Bruno Tonioli on both of their dances during the Nov. 17 semifinals.

"Sometimes when people are doing so well in the competition, people don't necessarily vote," Julianne told the duo, "because they think you're doing so well with scores."

And the pair did do well, earning 30 out of 30 points on both their paso doble set to Rihanna 's "We Found Love" as well as their quickstep to Amy Winehouse 's "Valerie." The combined 60 points from the judges put them at the top of the leader board alongside Amber Glenn and partner Pasha Pashkov , who also earned a perfect 60.

"I want to say you have been dealing with everything with grace, with the noise outside," he told her, "and teaching me the things that I have only dreamed of to learn."

The Western Australian singer, songwriter, multi-instrumentalist and Tame Impala spearhead will receive the second annual ARIA Global Impact Award, announced ahead of the 40 th annual ARIAs this Wednesday, Nov. 18.

“I just found out I am this year’s recipient of the Global Impact Award at the ARIAs, which is huge, it’s such an honor, obviously,” enthuses Parker, whose career collection of ARIAs now lifts to 14. “I’m going to be at the ARIA Awards to receive it in person, so I’ll see you there. Thank you.” Related Noah Kahan Reacts to 2027 Grammy Nominations Snub: 'I Was In My Feelings for a Sec' 'Grand Theft Auto VI' Revs Its Engines & Leads 2026 Game Awards Nominations: Full List Cody Johnson on Why He's Skipping 2026 CMA Awards: 'Going 100 MPH All the Time Isn't Healthy'

Parker has “spent nearly 20 years making records that the rest of the world can’t stop playing. Rihanna has covered him, Lady Gaga and Dua Lipa have brought him into the studio and this year Dracula sank its teeth into the ARIA Top 10 for 18 weeks,” remarks ARIA CEO Annabelle Herd. “He’s shown a generation of Australian artists that a song made in a home studio in Perth can find its biggest audiences in America, Britain, Mexico and Brazil. Dom Dolla was the inaugural recipient of the award , which is presented at the discretion of the ARIA board to an artist whose international efforts are said to exemplify Australia’s influence in contemporary music worldwide.

entertainment.body:
It's clear that Y2K fashion isn't a temporary trend, it's a lasting resurgence. That's particularly true when it comes to jeans.

While several early aughts denim designs have made their way back into our closets, from rhinestone styles to baggy silhouettes and low-slung fits, one has remained underrated— the bootcut jean.

Based on runways and street style pics alike, bootcut jeans are poised for a potential 2027 takeover. The best part? You can save on the rising trend now because we found tons of pairs on sale for Black Friday, from $50.

Before skinny jeans stepped onto the scene, bootcut jeans were the denim of choice throughout the early to mid aughts.

While bootcut jeans can technically be low-rise, we're mostly referring to its silhouette, which is somewhere between a flare and straight leg jean. With a slim fit through the hips and thighs, bootcut jeans boast a leg-elongating, curve-defining fit compared to the effortless laidback feel offered by baggy jeans with low-slung waists.

"NCIS: Origins" gave us a double dose of Mike Franks this week.

Muse Watson returned to play the elder version of Gibbs' friend and mentor in Tuesday's episode, appearing to Gibbs in a vision after he fell unconscious. (Watson's Franks died back in Season 8 of " NCIS ," but came back in a number of flashbacks after that.) Plus, we saw the '90s version of Franks — played by Kyle Schmid — take on a tough case of a wife and mom escaping an abusive husband... and bend the rules to make sure justice was served.

TVLine chatted with Watson and Schmid about Franks' double duty this week, and they opened up about watching each other play Franks, Watson acting alongside Mark Harmon again for the first time in years, and the "action-packed" final episodes of Season 3.

TVLINE | We got the rare opportunity to see two versions of Franks on screen this week. Kyle, do you take any pointers on how to play Franks when you're watching Muse in action? SCHMID | I took every pointer I could when we first started the show. [Mark] Harmon was generous to set me up with Muse, and we got together and had countless phone calls in the beginning and just talked about life and the way we saw the world and approached acting and the role. For me, it was very easy to see why Franks had become such a beloved character on the show, because it was kind of curated by Muse, and Muse himself is such a dedicated actor, a proud father, just a generous human being who strives to be the best version of himself as possible. That's what I got from my time being able to study Muse when we first started, and it occurred to me in that time frame: That is what Franks is. Franks is the best version of himself that he can be, with the way that he sees the world, and is willing to do anything for the people in the family that surround him, and it's just a pleasure being able to work with somebody like Muse.

CBS TVLINE | Muse, what do you think about Kyle's take on Franks? Does he bring out a different side of the character than you imagined? WATSON | No, not really. [ Laughs ] He nails it. And I was tickled to death. When I came to town, I was an actor, and I wanted to play different roles, so I worked really hard on playing different roles. I based this guy on my Uncle Charles, who was a Marine, and he was a real Mike Franks. And I was so tickled to death when I realized, talking to Kyle on the phone, that Kyle was an actor, and that he approached it the same way I did. I've watched his performances, and he's just incredible. I couldn't be any prouder.
